prompt: Which statement correctly describes the two objects created when an application is registered in Microsoft Entra ID?
choices: An application object (the global blueprint) and, per tenant, a service principal (the local, governable instance)
A service principal and a Conditional Access policy
A managed identity and an app registration, with no service principal involved
An enterprise application and a Key Vault access policy
correctAnswers: An application object (the global blueprint) and, per tenant, a service principal (the local, governable instance)
explanation: Registration always produces an application object plus a service principal per consuming tenant. Conditional Access policies and Key Vault access policies are unrelated objects.

prompt: What does the app registration primarily define?
choices: What the app is and can request: redirect URIs, certificates/secrets, and requested API permissions
Which users and groups are assigned to use the app in this tenant
The RBAC role assignments granted to the app's service principal
The Conditional Access policy scoped to the app
correctAnswers: What the app is and can request: redirect URIs, certificates/secrets, and requested API permissions
explanation: The app registration is the blueprint of the app itself. User/group assignment, RBAC, and Conditional Access are all local, tenant-specific governance handled through the enterprise application (service principal).

prompt: Under which portal blade do you govern a service principal's assigned users, SSO configuration, and granted (not just requested) permissions in a given tenant?
choices: Enterprise applications
App registrations
Privileged Identity Management
Key Vault access policies
correctAnswers: Enterprise applications
explanation: Enterprise applications is where the local service principal is governed: assignments, SSO, Conditional Access, and actually-granted permissions. App registrations only defines what's requested.

prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS app is consented to by three different customer tenants. How many service principals exist for that single app registration?
choices: Three — one service principal per consuming tenant
One — service principals are global, not per tenant
Zero — multi-tenant apps don't use service principals
Three app registrations and one shared service principal
correctAnswers: Three — one service principal per consuming tenant
explanation: Each tenant that consents to a multi-tenant app gets its own local service principal instance, even though there is only one underlying application object.

prompt: A delegated permission is granted to an application. What can that application do with it?
choices: Act on behalf of the signed-in user, limited to what that user could do themselves
Act as itself with no user context, regardless of any user's own permissions
Bypass all Conditional Access policies automatically
Access every mailbox in the tenant without further consent
correctAnswers: Act on behalf of the signed-in user, limited to what that user could do themselves
explanation: Delegated permissions are bounded by the signed-in user's own access. Acting with no user context describes application permissions instead.

prompt: An application is granted the Mail.Read application permission. What does this allow?
choices: The app can read mail as itself, without any signed-in user, subject to admin consent
The app can only read the mail of the user who is currently signed in
The permission is automatically limited to the app's own tenant
The permission requires no consent because it is scoped to Mail.Read
correctAnswers: The app can read mail as itself, without any signed-in user, subject to admin consent
explanation: Application permissions act as the app, independent of any user, and require admin consent regardless of the specific scope name.

prompt: Which statement about consenting to application permissions is correct?
choices: Application permissions always require admin consent, since no user is present to consent themselves
Application permissions can be consented to by any licensed user
Application permissions are consented to automatically the first time the app signs in
Application permissions never require consent if the app is single-tenant
correctAnswers: Application permissions always require admin consent, since no user is present to consent themselves
explanation: With no signed-in user present, only an administrator can grant consent for application permissions — this is true regardless of the app's tenancy model.

prompt: An administrator grants admin consent for an application's Mail.ReadWrite application permission. What is the scope of that consent?
choices: It applies tenant-wide, to every user, not just the administrator granting it
It applies only to the administrator's own mailbox
It applies only to users who individually re-consent afterward
It expires automatically after 90 days unless renewed
correctAnswers: It applies tenant-wide, to every user, not just the administrator granting it
explanation: Admin consent for an application permission is a tenant-wide grant. It doesn't limit itself to the approver's own data, require per-user re-consent, or expire on a fixed schedule by default.

prompt: Which User consent setting is recommended to reduce the risk of illicit consent grant attacks while still allowing convenience for low-risk apps?
choices: Allow user consent only for apps from verified publishers and for permissions classified as low impact
Allow user consent for any app requesting any permission
Disable user consent and also disable the admin consent workflow
Allow user consent only on weekends
correctAnswers: Allow user consent only for apps from verified publishers and for permissions classified as low impact
explanation: Restricting to verified publishers plus low-impact permissions balances convenience and risk. Disabling both user and admin consent workflows would block legitimate access requests entirely.

prompt: A user tries to sign in to an app requiring a permission they cannot consent to themselves. What happens if the admin consent workflow is enabled?
choices: The user can request access, and the request is routed to designated reviewers for approval
The sign-in silently fails with no way to request access
The user is automatically granted the permission after 24 hours
The app registration is automatically deleted
correctAnswers: The user can request access, and the request is routed to designated reviewers for approval
explanation: The admin consent workflow gives blocked users a path to request access rather than a dead end, routing the decision to named reviewers.

prompt: What attack does the admin consent workflow (routing requests to reviewers) primarily defend against?
choices: Illicit consent grant attacks, where a malicious app tricks a user into granting broad access
Brute-force password attacks against user accounts
SIM-swap attacks against SMS-based MFA
Ransomware encryption of on-premises file shares
correctAnswers: Illicit consent grant attacks, where a malicious app tricks a user into granting broad access
explanation: Requiring admin review before high-impact consent is granted closes the door on illicit consent grant attacks. It has no bearing on password brute-forcing, SIM-swap, or ransomware.

prompt: Where can an administrator review which OAuth permissions have actually been granted to an app, as opposed to only what it requests?
choices: Enterprise applications ▸ Permissions
App registrations ▸ Certificates & secrets
Key Vault ▸ Access configuration
Conditional Access ▸ Policies
correctAnswers: Enterprise applications ▸ Permissions
explanation: Granted permissions (the actual consent record) live on the enterprise application. Certificates & secrets is unrelated, and the other two options belong to entirely different services.

prompt: During a permissions review, you find an app has an unused Mail.ReadWrite application permission granted tenant-wide. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Remove the unused high-privilege grant, since application permissions act without user context and carry outsized risk
Leave it, since application permissions are always lower-risk than delegated permissions
Convert it to a delegated permission automatically
Ignore it because application permissions cannot be revoked once granted
correctAnswers: Remove the unused high-privilege grant, since application permissions act without user context and carry outsized risk
explanation: Unused high-privilege application-permission grants should be revoked as part of least-privilege hygiene; they can absolutely be removed, and they are generally higher-risk than delegated permissions, not lower.

prompt: What is the defining characteristic of a managed identity compared to a regular service principal?
choices: Azure automatically creates and rotates its credentials — there is no secret or certificate to manage
It can only be used by Azure Functions
It requires a Conditional Access policy to function
It can only hold delegated permissions, never application permissions
correctAnswers: Azure automatically creates and rotates its credentials — there is no secret or certificate to manage
explanation: The defining benefit of a managed identity is Azure-managed credentials. It is not restricted to a single resource type, doesn't require CA to work, and can be granted application permissions like Mail.Read.

prompt: Which lifecycle statement is correct for a system-assigned managed identity?
choices: It is created with, and deleted automatically when, its single host resource is deleted
It exists as an independent Azure resource that survives its host's deletion
It can be attached to multiple resources simultaneously
It requires a certificate to be uploaded before use
correctAnswers: It is created with, and deleted automatically when, its single host resource is deleted
explanation: System-assigned identities are strictly 1:1 with their host and share its lifecycle. Independent survival and multi-resource attachment describe user-assigned identities instead.

prompt: Which lifecycle statement is correct for a user-assigned managed identity?
choices: It exists as its own standalone Azure resource and can be attached to multiple resources
It is automatically deleted whenever any one of its attached resources is deleted
It can only ever be attached to exactly one resource, like a system-assigned identity
It cannot be used to authenticate to Key Vault
correctAnswers: It exists as its own standalone Azure resource and can be attached to multiple resources
explanation: User-assigned identities are independent resources that outlive any single attached resource, and can be reused across many resources — the opposite of a system-assigned identity's 1:1 lifecycle.

prompt: Ten Azure Functions apps in a fleet all need the same identity to call a downstream API. Which managed identity type best fits this need?
choices: A single user-assigned managed identity attached to all ten function apps
Ten separate system-assigned managed identities, one per function app
A single system-assigned managed identity shared across all function apps
A service principal with a client secret shared via a configuration file
correctAnswers: A single user-assigned managed identity attached to all ten function apps
explanation: User-assigned identities are standalone and attachable to many resources — ideal for a shared identity across a fleet. System-assigned is strictly 1:1 and cannot be shared.

prompt: To let a VM read a secret from Azure Key Vault without storing any credential on the VM, which combination of steps is correct?
choices: Enable a managed identity on the VM, then grant that identity the Key Vault Secrets User role (or equivalent access policy) on the vault
Store the vault's master key in the VM's application settings, then restart the VM
Create a service principal with a client secret and embed it in the VM's startup script
Enable Conditional Access for the VM's IP address range
correctAnswers: Enable a managed identity on the VM, then grant that identity the Key Vault Secrets User role (or equivalent access policy) on the vault
explanation: Managed identity plus an RBAC grant achieves credential-free access. The other options all reintroduce a stored secret or misapply Conditional Access, which doesn't govern vault authorization.

prompt: Which Azure RBAC role is commonly granted to a managed identity that only needs to read secret values from a Key Vault?
choices: Key Vault Secrets User
Key Vault Administrator
Owner
Contributor
correctAnswers: Key Vault Secrets User
explanation: Key Vault Secrets User grants get/list on secrets without administrative control. Administrator, Owner, and Contributor all grant far more than the stated need.

prompt: Microsoft's recommended preference order for workload authentication, from most to least preferred, is:
choices: Managed identity, then service principal with certificate, then service principal with client secret
Service principal with client secret, then managed identity, then certificate-based service principal
Certificate-based service principal, then client secret, then managed identity
There is no preference; all three are equally recommended
correctAnswers: Managed identity, then service principal with certificate, then service principal with client secret
explanation: Managed identity removes stored credentials entirely and is always preferred when supported, followed by certificate-based, then secret-based service principals as fallbacks.

prompt: What does the acronym SPN commonly refer to in the context of Entra application identities?
choices: Service Principal Name/object, the local security identity representing an app in a tenant
A Security Policy Notification sent by Conditional Access
A Secrets Provisioning Node used by Key Vault
A Signed Permission Notice required for admin consent
correctAnswers: Service Principal Name/object, the local security identity representing an app in a tenant
explanation: SPN refers to the service principal representing an app locally in a tenant. The other definitions are invented and don't correspond to real Entra or Key Vault concepts.

prompt: Which statement about credential responsibility is correct for a standard (non-managed-identity) service principal?
choices: You are responsible for creating, storing, and rotating its secrets or certificates
Azure automatically rotates its credentials with no action required
It has no credentials at all and authenticates anonymously
Its credentials are stored in Conditional Access, not in Entra ID
correctAnswers: You are responsible for creating, storing, and rotating its secrets or certificates
explanation: Unlike a managed identity, a standard service principal's credentials are entirely your responsibility to manage and rotate.

prompt: A developer registers a new application that will later be published to multiple customer tenants. In which tenant does the app registration (the application object) live?
choices: The developer's home/origin tenant where it was registered
Every tenant that later consents to the app
No tenant — app registrations are global objects with no home tenant
The tenant of the first user who signs in to the app
correctAnswers: The developer's home/origin tenant where it was registered
explanation: The application object lives only in the tenant where it was originally registered; consuming tenants each only get a local service principal.

prompt: A user consents to a third-party app requesting delegated access to their calendar. What exactly is being granted?
choices: The app may act as that specific user, limited to what the user could do in their own calendar
The app gains application-level access to every user's calendar in the tenant
The consent automatically also grants admin consent for the whole tenant
The app receives a client secret that only the user can see
correctAnswers: The app may act as that specific user, limited to what the user could do in their own calendar
explanation: Delegated user consent is scoped to that one user's own data — it does not expand to tenant-wide or admin-level access.

prompt: Which of these best distinguishes 'requested' permissions from 'granted' permissions for an application?
choices: Requested permissions are declared on the app registration; granted permissions are the actual consent recorded on the service principal (enterprise application)
Requested and granted permissions are always identical and cannot differ
Granted permissions are visible only in Conditional Access logs
Requested permissions apply only to managed identities
correctAnswers: Requested permissions are declared on the app registration; granted permissions are the actual consent recorded on the service principal (enterprise application)
explanation: An app can request permissions it never receives consent for — the two lists can legitimately differ, and granted permissions surface under the enterprise application, not Conditional Access.

prompt: Which scenario is the strongest candidate for a system-assigned (rather than user-assigned) managed identity?
choices: A single Azure Function that needs its own dedicated identity with no other resource sharing it
A fleet of 50 VMs that must all present the same identity to a downstream API
An identity that must persist after the resource using it is deleted
An identity that needs to be pre-created before the resource exists
correctAnswers: A single Azure Function that needs its own dedicated identity with no other resource sharing it
explanation: A dedicated, non-shared, resource-tied identity is exactly the system-assigned use case. Sharing across many resources, surviving deletion, and pre-creation before the host exists all require user-assigned identities.

prompt: Which statement correctly differentiates delegated and application permissions in terms of consent requirements?
choices: Delegated permissions can sometimes be user-consented for low-risk scopes; application permissions always require admin consent
Both permission types always require admin consent with no exceptions
Delegated permissions always require admin consent; application permissions never do
Neither permission type requires any consent once the app is registered
correctAnswers: Delegated permissions can sometimes be user-consented for low-risk scopes; application permissions always require admin consent
explanation: Delegated permissions can be user-consented depending on policy and scope risk; application permissions have no user context to consent, so admin consent is always required.

prompt: An administrator wants to prevent end users from ever granting consent to new third-party apps, routing every request to a security reviewer instead. Which combination of settings achieves this?
choices: Set user consent to 'Do not allow user consent' and enable the admin consent workflow with named reviewers
Set user consent to 'Allow user consent for all apps' and disable the admin consent workflow
Enable Conditional Access requiring MFA for all sign-ins
Assign every user the Application Administrator Entra role
correctAnswers: Set user consent to 'Do not allow user consent' and enable the admin consent workflow with named reviewers
explanation: Disabling user consent removes the self-service path entirely, and the admin consent workflow gives users a reviewed path instead. MFA and directory role assignment don't affect the consent decision.

prompt: Which two statements about managed identities are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: Azure automatically rotates their credentials
System-assigned identities can be attached to multiple resources
User-assigned identities exist as standalone Azure resources
They require a client secret to be configured manually
correctAnswers: Azure automatically rotates their credentials
User-assigned identities exist as standalone Azure resources
explanation: System-assigned identities are strictly 1:1 and cannot be shared, and managed identities never require a manually configured secret at all.

prompt: Which two are true about application permissions (as opposed to delegated permissions)? (Choose two.)
choices: They always require admin consent
They act without any signed-in user context
They are automatically scoped to the consenting user's own data
They can be consented to by any standard user
correctAnswers: They always require admin consent
They act without any signed-in user context
explanation: Being scoped to a consenting user's own data and being consentable by any standard user both describe delegated permissions, not application permissions.

prompt: Which two settings should typically be reviewed and hardened to reduce the risk of illicit consent grant attacks? (Choose two.)
choices: User consent settings (restrict to verified publishers / low-impact permissions)
Admin consent workflow (named reviewers for requests)
Storage account public blob access
Network security group inbound rules
correctAnswers: User consent settings (restrict to verified publishers / low-impact permissions)
Admin consent workflow (named reviewers for requests)
explanation: Both settings directly control who can grant OAuth consent. Storage public access and NSG rules are unrelated network/storage controls.

prompt: Referring to requirement 2 (a nightly invoicing daemon with no signed-in user must read all mailboxes via Microsoft Graph, with access reviewable and visible to admins, not silently expandable by end users), which permission and consent configuration is correct?
choices: Grant the daemon's app registration the Mail.Read application permission with admin consent, and review it periodically under Enterprise applications ▸ Permissions
Grant the daemon's app the Mail.Read delegated permission and let end users consent individually
Enable user consent for all apps from any publisher so the daemon can self-consent at runtime
Assign the daemon's service principal the Global Administrator Entra role
correctAnswers: Grant the daemon's app registration the Mail.Read application permission with admin consent, and review it periodically under Enterprise applications ▸ Permissions
explanation: A daemon has no signed-in user, so it needs an application permission, which always requires admin consent — creating a reviewable, tenant-wide grant. Delegated permission, broad user consent, and an overbroad directory role are all wrong fits.

prompt: Referring to requirement 2, why is a delegated permission unsuitable for the nightly invoicing daemon?
choices: Delegated permissions require a signed-in user context, which a nightly unattended daemon does not have
Delegated permissions cannot be scoped to Mail.Read under any circumstances
Delegated permissions are always more privileged than application permissions
Delegated permissions cannot be consented to by an administrator
correctAnswers: Delegated permissions require a signed-in user context, which a nightly unattended daemon does not have
explanation: The daemon runs with no signed-in user, which is precisely the scenario application permissions exist for. Delegated permissions depend on a user context by design.

prompt: Referring to requirement 3 (the deployment pipeline on an Azure VM must retrieve a Key Vault secret with no client secret stored on the VM or in code), which identity approach is correct?
choices: Enable a system-assigned managed identity on the VM and grant it a Key Vault RBAC role
Create a service principal with a client secret and store the secret in an environment variable on the VM
Embed the Key Vault master key directly in the pipeline's YAML file
Grant the VM's local administrator account access via a Key Vault access policy
correctAnswers: Enable a system-assigned managed identity on the VM and grant it a Key Vault RBAC role
explanation: Managed identity removes the need for any stored client secret. The other options all reintroduce a stored secret, which the requirement explicitly rules out.

prompt: Proposed solution: Register an app, request the Mail.Read delegated permission, and have the on-call engineer sign in interactively once a day to refresh the token for the background job. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: This still depends on a signed-in user and a delegated scope tied to that user, and is not a true unattended, admin-reviewable application-level grant — it's fragile and doesn't match the stated goal.

prompt: Proposed solution: Register an app, request the Mail.Read application permission, obtain tenant-wide admin consent from a designated administrator, and periodically review the grant under Enterprise applications ▸ Permissions. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: Yes
explanation: This is exactly the pattern for an unattended background job: an application permission with admin consent, visible and reviewable by administrators.

prompt: Proposed solution: Enable user consent for all apps and permissions tenant-wide so the background job's service account can self-consent to Mail.Read the first time it runs. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: Broad user consent lets grants expand silently without admin review, directly violating the requirement that access not be silently expandable by end users.

prompt: Order the steps an administrator follows to grant a daemon app admin-consented application permissions to Microsoft Graph.
reorderItems: Register the application under App registrations
Add the required application permission (e.g., Mail.Read) under API permissions
Verify the resulting grant under Enterprise applications ▸ Permissions
Periodically review the grant for continued need
explanation: The app must exist and declare the permission before consent can be granted; the grant is verified afterward on the service principal, and reviewed on an ongoing basis.

prompt: Order the steps to move a VM-hosted workload from a service principal with a client secret to a managed identity.
reorderItems: Enable a system-assigned (or attach a user-assigned) managed identity on the VM
Grant the managed identity the required RBAC role on the target resource (e.g., Key Vault)
Update the application code to acquire tokens via the managed identity endpoint instead of a client secret
Remove the old client secret from configuration and revoke it on the service principal
Confirm the workload authenticates successfully with no stored secret remaining
explanation: The identity must exist and be authorized before the code can rely on it; only once the new path is confirmed working should the old secret be revoked.

prompt: Configure this simplified API permissions screen for a nightly daemon app that must read all mailboxes with no signed-in user, ensuring the grant is properly consented at the tenant level.
explanation: The daemon has no signed-in user, so it requires an application permission, which must carry tenant-wide admin consent to function correctly.
